\chapter{How Are You?}
\label{ch:how-are-you}
\hlchaptermodality{3}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask how someone is in German, answer naturally, and return the question.}

German asks after someone with a verb of motion — Wie geht es dir?, \textquotedblleft{}how goes it to you?\textquotedblright{} — so this chapter builds that question one word at a time and then answers it across a full ladder, from Sehr gut! down through Es geht and So lala to Nicht so gut. Around it sit the two courtesies that hold every German conversation together, danke and bitte, each an English word in disguise. GE-C03-formal-practice runs the finished exchange in the formal register, where only the listener word changes.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[danke]{danke — \textquotedblleft{}thank you,\textquotedblright{} which is really \textquotedblleft{}I think of you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C03-danke}



\begin{quote}
You can introduce yourself in German. Next comes \emph{how are you?} — and every answer to it leans on one word. It hides a secret that English shares and hides too: \textbf{to thank is to think.}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: danke}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{danke} — \textquotedblleft{}thank you.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-a-german} — \emph{DAHN-kuh}: a pure open \emph{ah}, the vowel of English \emph{father}, and a final \emph{-e} that sinks to a soft \emph{uh} rather than disappearing. Stress the front: \emph{DAHN-kuh}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{danke} comes from \textbf{denken}, \textquotedblleft{}to think.\textquotedblright{} The old idea: to thank someone is to \textbf{keep them in mind} — \textquotedblleft{}I think of you,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}you are in my thoughts.\textquotedblright{} German \emph{Dank} (\textquotedblleft{}thanks\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{Gedanke} (\textquotedblleft{}a thought\textquotedblright{}) are the same root wearing two coats.

And here is the payoff for an English speaker: \textbf{English \textquotedblleft{}thank\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}think\textquotedblright{} are the same word too.} Old English \emph{þancian} (\textquotedblleft{}thank\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{þencan} (\textquotedblleft{}think\textquotedblright{}) split from one root — to thank was to \emph{hold in thought}. So \emph{danke} is not foreign at all; it is English \textbf{thank} with the \textbf{think} still visible inside it.

Three different pictures of gratitude, worth holding side by side:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Thanks\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{Literal idea} \\
\midrule
German & \emph{danke} & \textquotedblleft{}I \textbf{think} of you\textquotedblright{} \\
French & \emph{merci} & a \textbf{reward}, a \textbf{mercy} \\
Spanish & \emph{gracias} & \textbf{grace}, \textbf{favour} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}danke\textquotedblright{} — \emph{DAHN-kuh}, stress the front
  \item \textquotedblleft{}danke\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}denken\textquotedblright{} — thanks, and the thinking inside it
  \item English \textquotedblleft{}thank\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}think\textquotedblright{} — one root, two coats
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What everyday verb is \emph{danke} built from? (\emph{Denken}, \textquotedblleft{}to think.\textquotedblright{}) What two English words share that same split? (\emph{Thank} and \emph{think}.) Where does the stress fall? (On the front: \emph{DAHN-kuh}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[schön]{schön — \textquotedblleft{}beautiful,\textquotedblright{} and your first umlaut with rounded lips}

\label{lesson:GE-C03-schoen}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Danke} on its own is complete and polite. But German has a one-word upgrade, and the upgrading word is worth having on its own — it is one of the commonest adjectives in the language.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: schön}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{schön} — \textquotedblleft{}beautiful, lovely, nice.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{umlaut-oe} — \textbf{ö} is made by saying \textbf{ay} and then \emph{rounding your lips} as if to whistle, without moving your tongue. English has no such vowel, so build it from two things you can already do: hold the \emph{e} of \emph{bed}, then push your lips forward into an \emph{o} shape. That is \textbf{ö}.
  \item \texttt{sch-sh} — \textbf{sch} is simply English \textbf{sh}. So \emph{schön} is \emph{shurn} — with no \emph{r} actually sounded, the way a Southern English speaker says \emph{fern}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{schön} is English \textbf{sheen}. Both come from a Germanic root meaning \emph{bright, shining} — so the oldest sense of \emph{schön} is not \textquotedblleft{}pretty\textquotedblright{} but \textquotedblleft{}gleaming,\textquotedblright{} and English kept the shine while German took the beauty.

Now snap it onto the word you already have:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{danke schön} — \textquotedblleft{}thank you nicely\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}thank you very much.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Literally you are thanking someone \emph{beautifully}. English has no equivalent move; the nearest is the tone of voice in \textquotedblleft{}thanks \emph{so} much.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ay\textquotedblright{} then round your lips — \textquotedblleft{}ö\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}schön\textquotedblright{} (\emph{shurn})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}danke schön\textquotedblright{} — thank you very much
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{schön} mean, and which English word is it? (\textquotedblleft{}Beautiful\textquotedblright{}; \emph{sheen}.) How do you make \textbf{ö}? (Say \emph{ay}, then round the lips.) Upgrade a thank-you. (\emph{Danke schön}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vielen Dank]{vielen Dank — \textquotedblleft{}many thanks,\textquotedblright{} with the noun stepping forward}

\label{lesson:GE-C03-vielen-dank}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Danke} is a verb form — \textquotedblleft{}I thank.\textquotedblright{} But English also has a \emph{noun}, \textbf{thanks}, and so does German. Meet it, and a second upgrade opens up.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der Dank}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der Dank} — \textquotedblleft{}the thanks, the gratitude\textquotedblright{} (masculine).
\end{quote}

Capital \textbf{D}, because every German noun is capitalised — the rule from \emph{Tag}. Said \emph{dahnk}, with the final \textbf{k} crisp.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{viel} means \textquotedblleft{}much,\textquotedblright{} and it is English \textbf{full} — a full measure of something. Put it in front of \emph{Dank} and you get the phrase Germans reach for when \emph{danke} alone feels too thin:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{vielen Dank} — \textquotedblleft{}many thanks.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The \textbf{-en} on \emph{vielen} is the same kind of adjective ending you met on \emph{guten Tag}: German adjectives dress to match their noun. You do not have to build it yet — learn \emph{vielen Dank} whole, the way you learned \emph{guten Tag} whole.

So the family now reads: \emph{danke} (I thank) · \emph{der Dank} (the thanks) · \emph{Gedanke} (a thought) — all from \emph{denken}, \textquotedblleft{}to think.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Dank\textquotedblright{} — the noun, capital D
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vielen Dank\textquotedblright{} — many thanks
  \item the family — \textquotedblleft{}danke\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}Dank\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}denken\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the noun behind \emph{danke}? (\emph{Der Dank}.) What English word is \emph{viel}? (\emph{Full} — a full measure.) Say \textquotedblleft{}many thanks.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Vielen Dank}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bitte]{bitte — the Swiss-army word: \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{} \emph{and} \textquotedblleft{}you're welcome\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C03-bitte}



\begin{quote}
Every \emph{danke} wants an answer. German's answer is a word that also means \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{} — and three other things besides, all from one idea.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: bitte}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{bitte} — \textquotedblleft{}please,\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}you're welcome.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{i-short} — \emph{BIT-tuh}: a short crisp \emph{i} as in English \emph{bit}, a clearly doubled \emph{t}, and the soft \emph{-uh} ending you already met on \emph{danke}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{bitte} is the asking-form of \textbf{bitten}, \textquotedblleft{}to ask, to request, to pray.\textquotedblright{} When you say \emph{bitte} you are, at root, \textbf{making a request} — \textquotedblleft{}I ask this of you.\textquotedblright{}

That verb is a close cousin of two English words:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{bid} — as in \textquotedblleft{}I \emph{bid} you welcome,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}do as you are \emph{bidden}\textquotedblright{}: to ask or command.
  \item \textbf{bead} — astonishingly, yes. A \emph{bead} was originally a \textbf{prayer}. People counted their prayers (Old English \emph{gebed}) on a string, and the name of the prayer slid onto the little ball it was counted on. A rosary \textbf{bead} is a frozen request — exactly what \emph{bitte} still is.
\end{itemize}

That single idea, \emph{I ask}, is what lets one word cover so much ground:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{You say \emph{bitte} when…} & \textbf{It means} & \textbf{Why it is all \textquotedblleft{}I ask\textquotedblright{}} \\
\midrule
making a request & \textbf{please} & \textquotedblleft{}I ask you…\textquotedblright{} \\
answering \emph{danke} & \textbf{you're welcome} & \textquotedblleft{}I ask nothing back\textquotedblright{} \\
handing something over & \textbf{here you go} & \textquotedblleft{}I offer, at your request\textquotedblright{} \\
you did not hear & \textbf{pardon?} & \textquotedblleft{}I ask you to repeat\textquotedblright{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Tone does the sorting. The word never changes.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The courtesy loop closes every small favour in German: \textbf{Danke.} — \textbf{Bitte.} It is the twin of Spanish \emph{de nada} and French \emph{de rien}, and leaving off the \emph{bitte} sounds curt in a way English \textquotedblleft{}no problem\textquotedblright{} does not.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bitte\textquotedblright{} — \emph{BIT-tuh}, doubled \emph{t}
  \item the loop — \textquotedblleft{}danke\textquotedblright{} … \textquotedblleft{}bitte\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bitte\textquotedblright{} as \emph{please}, then as \emph{you're welcome} — same word, new tone
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What verb is \emph{bitte} from? (\emph{Bitten}, \textquotedblleft{}to ask, to pray.\textquotedblright{}) What two English words are its cousins? (\emph{Bid}, and \emph{bead} — a bead was a prayer.) Name two jobs \emph{bitte} does. (Please; you're welcome; here you go; pardon?) What answers \emph{danke}? (\emph{Bitte}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gehen]{gehen — \textquotedblleft{}to go,\textquotedblright{} and it is just English \emph{go}}

\label{lesson:GE-C03-gehen}



\begin{quote}
German asks \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} with a verb of \textbf{motion}. You already own that verb without having studied it, because it \emph{is} English \emph{go}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: gehen}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{gehen} — \textquotedblleft{}to go.\textquotedblright{} The form you will need most is \textbf{geht}, \textquotedblleft{}goes.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

That \textbf{-t} is the ending you already met on \emph{heißt}: third person, one person, one \emph{t}.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{h-silent-lengthening} — in \emph{gehen} the \textbf{h} is \textbf{not} breathed. It is a silent letter whose whole job is to \textbf{stretch the vowel before it}: \emph{GAY-en}, not \emph{ge-HEN}. So \textbf{geht} is simply \emph{gayt}.
\end{itemize}

This is worth banking now, because German uses the trick everywhere — \emph{sehr}, \emph{Ihnen}, \emph{Jahr} all hide a lengthening \emph{h}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{gehen} and English \textbf{go} descend from the \emph{same} Germanic verb — no Latin detour, no false friend, a straight cognate. When you say \emph{geht}, you are saying \emph{goes}.

And that is the whole idea behind German's \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{}: wellbeing is not something you \emph{are}, it is something that \textbf{goes}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{The verb it asks with} & \textbf{The picture} \\
\midrule
German & \emph{gehen}, \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{} & how does it \textbf{go}? \\
French & \emph{aller}, \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{} & how does it \textbf{go}? \\
Spanish & \emph{estar}, \textquotedblleft{}to stand\textquotedblright{} & how are you \textbf{standing}? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two of the three put wellbeing in motion; Spanish puts it on its feet.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gehen\textquotedblright{} (\emph{GAY-en}) — the \emph{h} only stretches
  \item \textquotedblleft{}geht\textquotedblright{} (\emph{gayt}) — \textquotedblleft{}goes\textquotedblright{}
  \item German \emph{gehen} and English \emph{go} — the same word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What English word is \emph{gehen}? (\emph{Go} — a straight cognate.) What does the \emph{h} do in \emph{gehen}? (Nothing but lengthen the vowel.) Which two of the three languages ask \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} with \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{}? (German and French; Spanish uses \textquotedblleft{}to stand.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[es]{es — \textquotedblleft{}it,\textquotedblright{} the small word German leans on}

\label{lesson:GE-C03-es}



\begin{quote}
You have the verb: \emph{geht}, \textquotedblleft{}goes.\textquotedblright{} But goes \emph{what}? German needs a subject, and for a state — the weather, your day — it reaches for one tiny word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: es}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{es} — \textquotedblleft{}it.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Said \emph{ess}: a short clean \emph{e}, the vowel of English \emph{bet}, and a crisp \emph{s}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{es} is English \textbf{it}. The two look unalike only because of the same swap you already met in \emph{das} / \emph{that}: where English keeps a \textbf{t}, German often shows an \textbf{s}. Line them up and the pattern is one column wide:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{German} \\
\midrule
tha\textbf{t} & da\textbf{s} \\
i\textbf{t} & e\textbf{s} \\
wha\textbf{t} & wa\textbf{s} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Same word, one consonant apart — and \emph{das}, the neuter \textquotedblleft{}the,\textquotedblright{} is \emph{es}'s close relative, which is why both point at things rather than people.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}es\textquotedblright{} (\emph{ess}) — \textquotedblleft{}it\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}it\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}es\textquotedblright{}; \textquotedblleft{}that\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}das\textquotedblright{} — the same t/s swap, twice
  \item \textquotedblleft{}es geht\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}it goes\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{es}? (\textquotedblleft{}It.\textquotedblright{}) Which English consonant turns up as \emph{s} in German? (\emph{T} — \emph{it/es}, \emph{that/das}, \emph{what/was}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}it goes.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Es geht}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mir]{mir — \textquotedblleft{}to me,\textquotedblright{} the third coat that \emph{ich} wears}

\label{lesson:GE-C03-mir}



\begin{quote}
You have \emph{ich} (\textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} the doer) and \emph{mich} (\textquotedblleft{}me,\textquotedblright{} the done-to). German keeps a \textbf{third} form for a different job — and English keeps the same job without a special word for it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: mir}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{mir} — \textquotedblleft{}to me, for me.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Said \emph{meer}: a long \emph{ee}, and a soft German \textbf{r} at the end that is barely more than a vowel — closer to \emph{mee-uh} than to an English \emph{meer}.

\begin{cousinweb}
German marks \emph{the person something happens \textbf{to}} with a form of its own. It is called the \textbf{dative} — the \textquotedblleft{}to-whom\textquotedblright{} form.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Job} & \textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
the doer & \emph{ich} & I \\
the done-to & \emph{mich} & me \\
the to-whom & \emph{mir} & to me \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English merged the last two into one word, \emph{me}, and now signals the difference by \textbf{word order} instead: \textquotedblleft{}she gave \textbf{me} the book\textquotedblright{} — \emph{me} is the to-whom there, even though it looks identical to the done-to \emph{me} in \textquotedblleft{}she saw me.\textquotedblright{} German never merged them, so it can put the to-whom anywhere and still be clear.

That is why wellbeing works the way it does: something \emph{goes}, and it goes \textbf{to a person}. The person is in the dative.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three coats — \textquotedblleft{}ich\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}mich\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}mir\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mir\textquotedblright{} (\emph{meer}) — \textquotedblleft{}to me\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}es geht mir\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}it goes to me\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{mir} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To me, for me.\textquotedblright{}) Which of \emph{ich} / \emph{mich} / \emph{mir} is the to-whom form? (\emph{Mir}.) How does English show that job instead? (By word order — \textquotedblleft{}gave \emph{me} the book.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dir]{dir — \textquotedblleft{}to you,\textquotedblright{} and English used to have it too}

\label{lesson:GE-C03-dir}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Mir} is \textquotedblleft{}to me.\textquotedblright{} To ask how someone else is doing, you need the same form pointed the other way.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dir}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{dir} — \textquotedblleft{}to you,\textquotedblright{} the to-whom form of \emph{du}.
\end{quote}

Said \emph{deer}, with the same soft trailing \textbf{r} as \emph{mir}. The two rhyme, which is the easiest way to remember they are a pair.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{dir} is English \textbf{thee} — the old to-you form, from the same Germanic root, with the \emph{th} hardened to \emph{d} exactly as \emph{das} answers \emph{that}.

English has not lost it entirely. It is fossilised in old phrases: \textquotedblleft{}I give \textbf{thee} thanks,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}woe is \textbf{thee}.\textquotedblright{} Those are datives — \emph{thee} was never the doer, always the to-whom, which is precisely \emph{dir}'s job.

So the pattern completes itself:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{doer} & \textbf{to-whom} \\
\midrule
\emph{ich} & \emph{mir} \\
\emph{du} & \emph{dir} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Remember: \emph{dir} belongs to \emph{du}, so it is for friends and family. A stranger gets a different word, and that is the next lesson.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mir\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}dir\textquotedblright{} — they rhyme
  \item \textquotedblleft{}du\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}dir\textquotedblright{} — doer, then to-whom
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dir\textquotedblright{} and English \textquotedblleft{}thee\textquotedblright{} — the same word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{dir} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To you.\textquotedblright{}) Which English word is it? (\emph{Thee}.) Whom do you say \emph{dir} to? (Someone you call \emph{du} — a friend or family.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Wie geht es dir?]{Wie geht es dir? — \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C03-wie-geht-es}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new is coming. You have all four words — \emph{wie}, \emph{geht}, \emph{es}, \emph{dir}. This lesson only puts them in order.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Wie geht es dir?}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Wie geht es dir?} — \textquotedblleft{}How are you?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Word for word: \textquotedblleft{}How goes it to you?\textquotedblright{}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{wie} & how \\
\emph{geht} & goes \\
\emph{es} & it \\
\emph{dir} & to you \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Said \emph{vee gayt es deer} — remember German \textbf{w} says \emph{v}, and \emph{ie} is a long \emph{ee}.

Every piece has been earned: \emph{wie} from asking someone's name, \emph{geht} from \emph{gehen}, \emph{es} and \emph{dir} from the last two lessons. This is what the book has been building toward — a real question assembled from parts, not memorised whole.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Wie geht's?}
In speech, \emph{geht es} crushes together into \textbf{geht's}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Wie geht's?} — the form you will actually hear.
\end{quote}

It drops the \emph{dir} entirely, which makes it neutral: no need to decide between friend and stranger. When in doubt, this is the safe one.

And you can already answer it:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Wie geht's? — Danke, gut!}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Wie geht es dir?\textquotedblright{} — \emph{vee gayt es deer}
  \item the four pieces — \textquotedblleft{}wie\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}geht\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}es\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}dir\textquotedblright{}
  \item the short form — \textquotedblleft{}Wie geht's?\textquotedblright{}
  \item the whole exchange — \textquotedblleft{}Wie geht's?\textquotedblright{} … \textquotedblleft{}Danke, gut!\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{Wie geht es dir?} say word for word? (\textquotedblleft{}How goes it to you?\textquotedblright{}) What contracts into \emph{geht's}? (\emph{Geht es}.) Why is \emph{Wie geht's?} the safe form? (It drops \emph{dir}, so it needs no friend-or-stranger choice.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Ihnen]{Ihnen — \textquotedblleft{}to you,\textquotedblright{} said at a respectful distance}

\label{lesson:GE-C03-ihnen}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Dir} is for a friend. But you already know German splits its \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} in two, and the polite half needs its own to-whom form.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Ihnen}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ihnen} — \textquotedblleft{}to you,\textquotedblright{} formal.
\end{quote}

Said \emph{EE-nen}: the \textbf{h} is silent and merely stretches the \emph{i} into a long \emph{ee}, the same trick as in \emph{gehen}. Stress the front.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Ihnen} is, underneath, \textquotedblleft{}to \textbf{them}.\textquotedblright{} German's polite \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} is the third-person plural borrowed wholesale: rather than address you directly, the language speaks of you as though you were a group — distance as respect. \emph{Sie} is \textquotedblleft{}they\textquotedblright{} used as \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}; \emph{Ihnen} is \textquotedblleft{}to them\textquotedblright{} used as \textquotedblleft{}to you.\textquotedblright{}

The capital letter is doing real work. Written small, \emph{ihnen} means \textquotedblleft{}to them\textquotedblright{} about actual other people. Written \textbf{Ihnen}, it is aimed at the person you are speaking to. Same sound, and only the page can tell them apart.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{to whom} & \textbf{informal} & \textbf{formal} \\
\midrule
you & \emph{dir} & \emph{Ihnen} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ihnen\textquotedblright{} (\emph{EE-nen}) — long \emph{ee}, silent \emph{h}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dir\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Ihnen\textquotedblright{} — friend, then stranger
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Sie\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Ihnen\textquotedblright{} — the polite pair
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{Ihnen} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To you,\textquotedblright{} formally.) What does it literally say? (\textquotedblleft{}To them.\textquotedblright{}) What does the capital \textbf{I} tell you? (It is aimed at the listener, not at other people.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Wie geht es Ihnen?]{Wie geht es Ihnen? — the same question, at a distance}

\label{lesson:GE-C03-wie-geht-register}



\begin{quote}
You have the question for a friend, and you have the formal to-whom word. Putting them together needs no new grammar at all — just a swap.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Wie geht es Ihnen?}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Wie geht es Ihnen?} — \textquotedblleft{}How are you?\textquotedblright{}, to a stranger or an elder.
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Listener} & \textbf{Question} \\
\midrule
friend, family & \emph{Wie geht es dir?} \\
stranger, elder & \emph{Wie geht es Ihnen?} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three of the four words never move. Only the last one changes.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: politeness lives in the pronoun}]
This is a rule worth generalising: \textbf{German carries politeness in the pronoun, not in the sentence.} English reaches for extra words to be polite — \textquotedblleft{}I was wondering whether you might…\textquotedblright{} — and stacks them in front. German usually leaves the sentence exactly as it is and changes \emph{who you are calling the person}.

You saw the same move with \emph{du} and \emph{Sie}. Here it reaches the dative: \emph{dir} becomes \emph{Ihnen}, and the politeness is done.

And when you would rather not choose at all, the contraction sidesteps it: \textbf{Wie geht's?} names no listener, so it commits to nothing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item to a friend — \textquotedblleft{}Wie geht es dir?\textquotedblright{}
  \item to a stranger — \textquotedblleft{}Wie geht es Ihnen?\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair back to back, hearing only the last word change
  \item the neutral escape — \textquotedblleft{}Wie geht's?\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the formal \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Wie geht es Ihnen?}) How many words change from the informal? (One — \emph{dir} to \emph{Ihnen}.) Where does German keep its politeness? (In the pronoun, not in extra words.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sehr]{sehr — \textquotedblleft{}very,\textquotedblright{} and it used to mean \textquotedblleft{}sorely\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C03-sehr}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Gut} answers \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} perfectly well. One small word in front of it turns a polite answer into a warm one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sehr}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{sehr} — \textquotedblleft{}very.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Said \emph{zair}: German \textbf{s} before a vowel buzzes like English \textbf{z}, the \textbf{h} is silent and stretches the vowel, and the \textbf{r} softens almost to \emph{ah}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Sehr gut!} — \textquotedblleft{}Very well!\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sehr} is English \textbf{sore}. In Middle High German it meant \emph{painfully, grievously} — and intensifiers very often start life as words for pain, then fade into pure degree. English did exactly the same thing and then half forgot: \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{sorely} missed,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{sore} afraid\textquotedblright{} both mean \emph{very}, not \emph{painful}.

So \emph{sehr gut} is, at the root, \textquotedblleft{}sorely good\textquotedblright{} — and English \emph{very} went the same road from a different start, having once meant \emph{truly} (French \emph{vrai}).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sehr\textquotedblright{} (\emph{zair}) — buzzing \emph{z}, silent \emph{h}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sehr gut\textquotedblright{} — very well
  \item \textquotedblleft{}danke sehr\textquotedblright{} — thanks very much
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{sehr} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Very.\textquotedblright{}) Which English word is it? (\emph{Sore} — as in \textquotedblleft{}sorely missed.\textquotedblright{}) Answer warmly. (\emph{Sehr gut!})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nicht]{nicht — \textquotedblleft{}not,\textquotedblright{} the same word as English \emph{naught}}

\label{lesson:GE-C03-nicht}



\begin{quote}
Not every day is a good one. To say so, you need the one word that turns any German sentence around.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: nicht}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{nicht} — \textquotedblleft{}not.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Said \emph{nikht}: the \textbf{ch} is the soft ich-sound from \emph{ich} and \emph{mich}, not the throat-scrape of \emph{Nacht}. The vowel before it is short.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{nicht} and English \textbf{not} are one word. Both come from a Germanic phrase meaning \emph{no thing at all} — literally \textquotedblleft{}not a whit.\textquotedblright{} English shows the longer form still: \textbf{naught} (and \textbf{nought}, the zero) is the undressed version, and \emph{not} is what happens when centuries of fast speech wear it down.

So the pair lines up with the \emph{ch} rule you already have:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{German} \\
\midrule
na\textbf{ugh}t & ni\textbf{ch}t \\
ni\textbf{gh}t & Na\textbf{ch}t \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That English \emph{gh} is a fossil: it once \emph{was} the German \emph{ch} sound, and English stopped pronouncing it while keeping the letters.

Now the answer ladder reaches downward:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Nicht so gut.} — \textquotedblleft{}Not so good.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nicht\textquotedblright{} (\emph{nikht}) — soft \emph{ch}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}naught\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}nicht\textquotedblright{}; \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Nacht\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nicht so gut\textquotedblright{} — not so good
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{nicht} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Not.\textquotedblright{}) Which English word is it, undressed? (\emph{Naught}.) What does English \emph{gh} used to be? (The German \emph{ch} sound.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[so lala]{so lala — \textquotedblleft{}so-so,\textquotedblright{} and the tune carries it}

\label{lesson:GE-C03-so-lala}



\begin{quote}
You can now say \emph{gut} and \emph{nicht so gut}. Between them sits the honest middle, and German fills it with a word that means nothing whatsoever.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: so lala}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{so lala} — \textquotedblleft{}so-so, middling, could be worse.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Said \emph{zo LAH-lah}, with the voice rising and falling across the \emph{lala} — a shrug set to music. Say it flat and it lands wrong; the tune is most of the meaning.

\begin{cousinweb}
There is nothing to take apart, and that is the point. \textbf{so} is English \textbf{so}. \textbf{lala} is not a word at all — it is the same \emph{lalala} you hum when you do not know the lyrics, pressed into service as a meaning.

This is not a German quirk. Reach for \textquotedblleft{}so-so\textquotedblright{} in almost any language and you find a small repeated noise doing the work, because a shrug is easier to sing than to say.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The shrug collection, four deep across the books in this series:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{The shrug} & \textbf{Literally} \\
\midrule
German & \emph{so lala} & \textquotedblleft{}so la-la\textquotedblright{} \\
French & \emph{comme ci, comme ça} & \textquotedblleft{}like this, like that\textquotedblright{} \\
Spanish & \emph{más o menos} & \textquotedblleft{}more or less\textquotedblright{} \\
Italian & \emph{così così} & \textquotedblleft{}so so\textquotedblright{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three of the four work by \textbf{repetition} — say a small thing twice and it comes out meaning \emph{neither one nor the other}.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}so lala\textquotedblright{} with the tune — up, then down
  \item the ladder — \textquotedblleft{}sehr gut\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}gut\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}so lala\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}nicht so gut\textquotedblright{}
  \item the four shrugs — \emph{so lala}, \emph{comme ci comme ça}, \emph{más o menos}, \emph{così così}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{so lala} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}So-so.\textquotedblright{}) What does \emph{lala} mean on its own? (Nothing — it is pure sing-song.) What do three of the four shrugs have in common? (They repeat a small word.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[es geht]{es geht — the German shrug: \textquotedblleft{}it goes\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C03-es-geht}



\begin{quote}
Someone asks \emph{Wie geht's?} You are neither great nor terrible. German has an answer for exactly that, and it is made of two words you already own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: es geht}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{es geht} — \textquotedblleft{}it goes.\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}So-so. I'm getting by.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Nothing has been added. That is the whole trick.

\emph{Es geht mir gut} says it goes \textbf{well}. Take the \emph{gut} away and German does not become vague — it becomes \emph{pointed}. The listener was waiting for a \emph{gut} or a \emph{schlecht}, and you gave neither. The \textbf{absence} is the meaning.

English does this too, with tone rather than deletion: \textquotedblleft{}It's… going.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the answer ladder}]
You now hold the whole range, top to bottom, with no word left unexplained:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Answer} & \textbf{Sense} \\
\midrule
\emph{Sehr gut!} & very well \\
\emph{Gut, danke.} & well, thanks \\
\emph{Es geht.} & so-so, getting by \\
\emph{So lala.} & so-so, sung with a shrug \\
\emph{Nicht so gut.} & not so well \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Es geht} and \emph{so lala} sit on the same rung and differ only in mood: \emph{es geht} is dry and a little stoic, \emph{so lala} is light and musical. Choose by the face you want to make.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}es geht\textquotedblright{} — flat, unhurried
  \item \textquotedblleft{}es geht mir gut\textquotedblright{}, then just \textquotedblleft{}es geht\textquotedblright{} — hear the \emph{gut} go missing
  \item the ladder top to bottom — \textquotedblleft{}Sehr gut\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}Gut danke\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}Es geht\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}So lala\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}Nicht so gut\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{es geht} mean literally, and in use? (\textquotedblleft{}It goes\textquotedblright{}; \textquotedblleft{}so-so.\textquotedblright{}) What makes it mean so-so? (The missing \emph{gut} — the absence is the message.) Which answer sits at the top of the ladder? (\emph{Sehr gut.}) At the bottom? (\emph{Nicht so gut.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[und]{und — \textquotedblleft{}and,\textquotedblright{} and how to hand the question back}

\label{lesson:GE-C03-und}



\begin{quote}
Someone asks how you are; you answer. A conversation only starts when you ask back — and German returns the question in two words.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: und}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{und} — \textquotedblleft{}and.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

It is English \textbf{and} with the vowel darkened, and it has barely changed in a thousand years — one of the oldest words either language still uses daily.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{d-t-final} — say \emph{oont}, not \emph{oond}. German hardens a \textbf{d} at the end of a word into a \textbf{t}. It is the same rule that makes \emph{Tag} come out as \emph{tock} rather than \emph{tahg}: whatever the spelling, a final consonant goes voiceless. So \emph{und} rhymes with English \emph{hunt}, not with \emph{shunned}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: returning the question}]
Hand the question back by naming the other person — in the \textbf{to-whom} form, because it is short for \textquotedblleft{}and how goes it \emph{to you}?\textquotedblright{}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{To a friend} & \textbf{To a stranger} \\
\midrule
\emph{und dir?} & \emph{und Ihnen?} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Not \emph{und du} — the dative is doing real work here, and using the doer-form is the giveaway of a beginner. The same shape appears across the series: Spanish \emph{¿y tú?}, French \emph{et toi?}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}und\textquotedblright{} (\emph{oont}, hard \emph{t})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}und dir?\textquotedblright{} — and you, to a friend
  \item \textquotedblleft{}und Ihnen?\textquotedblright{} — and you, to a stranger
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How is \emph{und} pronounced, and why? (\emph{Oont} — a final \emph{d} hardens to \emph{t}.) Return the question to a friend. (\emph{Und dir?}) To a stranger? (\emph{Und Ihnen?}) Why not \emph{und du}? (It is short for \textquotedblleft{}how goes it \emph{to you}\textquotedblright{} — the to-whom form.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — \emph{Wie geht's?}, casually}

\label{lesson:GE-C03-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Everything below has had its own lesson; this is the first time they run together at speed.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{Hallo! Wie geht's?} & Hi! How are you? \\
\emph{Gut, danke, und dir?} & Well, thanks — and you? \\
\emph{Es geht.} & So-so. \\
\emph{Danke!} — \emph{Bitte.} & Thanks! — You're welcome. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Four moves: greet, ask, answer-and-return, close the courtesy loop.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: why dir, and not du}]
\emph{Und dir?} keeps the dative because it is short for the full question — \textquotedblleft{}and how goes it \textbf{to you}?\textquotedblright{} Saying \emph{und du} would be the one wrong note in the whole exchange, and it is the commonest beginner slip there is.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the whole exchange, both voices
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Wie geht's? — Gut, danke.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Und dir? — Es geht.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Wie geht's? — Gut, danke, und dir?\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Run the casual exchange without looking. Which answer is the so-so one? (\emph{Es geht.}) Which word answers \emph{danke}? (\emph{Bitte.}) Why \emph{dir} and not \emph{du}? (The question means \textquotedblleft{}how goes it \emph{to you}\textquotedblright{} — the to-whom form.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Formal practice — \emph{Wie geht es Ihnen?}}

\label{lesson:GE-C03-formal-practice}



\begin{quote}
Same exchange, same order, same verb. One word changes throughout — and that is the chapter's whole argument about German politeness.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{Guten Tag. Wie geht es Ihnen?} & Good day. How are you? \\
\emph{Danke, gut. Und Ihnen?} & Well, thanks. And you? \\
\emph{Es geht.} & So-so. \\
\emph{Danke!} — \emph{Bitte.} & Thanks! — You're welcome. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Set it beside the casual version and the difference is two words, both of them the listener:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{Casual} & \textbf{Formal} \\
\midrule
the question & \emph{Wie geht's?} & \emph{Wie geht es Ihnen?} \\
the return & \emph{und dir?} & \emph{und Ihnen?} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Danke}, \emph{gut}, \emph{es geht} and \emph{bitte} do not shift at all. German courtesy words are register-neutral; the politeness is carried entirely by the pronoun.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the formal exchange, both voices
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Wie geht es Ihnen? — Danke, gut.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Und Ihnen? — Es geht.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Wie geht es Ihnen? — Danke, gut. Und Ihnen?\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which greeting opens the formal exchange? (\emph{Guten Tag.}) Which dative pronoun appears twice? (\emph{Ihnen.}) What changes from the casual version? (\emph{Dir} becomes \emph{Ihnen} — nothing else.) Where does German keep its politeness? (In the pronoun.)
\end{tcolorbox}
